cues.text: Section eight: digital ecosystems.
A digital ecosystem is a network of interdependent organisations, users, platforms and technologies that exchange services or data in order to create value.
Notice the emphasis on interdependence and exchange across several parties.
For that reason, a single internal application is not automatically an ecosystem.
One system used inside one organisation does not, by itself, make a network of interdependent participants.
Let us begin with the core concepts.
First, the API, which stands for application programming interface.
An API is an agreed interface through which software requests data or functionality.
Because other parties depend on it, authentication, permissions, versioning and error handling all matter.
Software must know who is asking, what that party may do, which version of the interface is in use, and what happens when something goes wrong.
Second, interoperability.
This means that systems can exchange information and correctly interpret it.
Exchange alone is not enough; the meaning must be understood.
So an API alone does not ensure interoperability if the participants disagree on what the data means.
Third, the platform business model.
A platform creates value by facilitating interactions among groups, such as merchants and customers, rather than producing every service internally.
Fourth, real-time data sharing.
This means timely updates across authorised participants.
It is not unrestricted access to all data.
The words "authorised" and "timely" both carry weight here.
Fifth, the ecosystem orchestrator.
This is the party that coordinates standards, partner relationships, security, access and performance.
Sixth, open innovation.
Here, partners and external developers contribute complementary services to the ecosystem.
Seventh, interdependence.
A participant's failure can affect others, so resilience must account for external dependencies, not only for what an organisation controls itself.
Now a worked fintech example.
Picture the flow like this.
The customer goes to the merchant checkout.
The merchant checkout connects to the payment platform.
The payment platform connects to the bank or payment network.
From there, a transaction status comes back, and that status leads on to merchant fulfilment.
In words: the platform authenticates the merchant, routes a payment request and reports the result.
The merchant fulfils an order only after verifying payment status.
Each participant contributes a capability.
Now a tutor supplement.
Webhooks can arrive twice or out of order.
Idempotency and reconciliation prevent duplicate fulfilment.
Idempotency means that handling the same message more than once does not produce a second effect, and reconciliation means checking records against each other to catch mismatches.
Timeouts, retries, signed callbacks and monitoring help manage integration failures.
These are practical illustrations of risk and interoperability, and they are not separate required S01 protocols.
The course uses Paystack and the Nigeria Immigration Service as examples of private and public ecosystem development respectively.

Other examples from the learning material include health records shared across authorised hospitals, laboratories and insurers; education platforms connected to payments and certification; and government identity and service integrations.
In every case, shared data must have a legitimate purpose and suitable access controls.
Next, the IT manager as ecosystem leader.
The role expands from internal system administration to strategic integration, partner governance, API agreements, data privacy, security and continuous improvement.
The manager should define service responsibilities, common standards, incident escalation, performance metrics and exit arrangements.
A zero-trust approach verifies access explicitly, rather than trusting a participant merely because it is connected.
Consider the benefits and the risks.
The benefits are faster innovation, broader market reach, reusable services and scaling through partnerships.
The risks are third-party outages, privacy breaches, incompatible standards, governance complexity and vendor lock-in.
AI, IoT, big data and blockchain can enable new services, but none of them is a mandatory component of every ecosystem.
Finally, the African context.
Opportunities include mobile-first adoption, regional innovation and public and private data collaboration.
Obstacles include rural infrastructure, inconsistent interoperability standards, cybersecurity exposure and legacy institutional habits.
The guiding advice is to design for inclusion, reliability and sustainable governance.
